A lesson of this site does not ask to be believed. Every statement that a
reader could take for a scientific result is marked as a **claim**, and each
claim names the evidence that supports it: a cell of the lesson that the
build runs again, a curated reference, a dataset card, a theorem that Lean
checks, or a recorded run of an agent that the build replays. A claim
without evidence, or with evidence that does not exist, stops the build, so
every claim on the site has its target. The claim's label says what kind of
evidence stands behind it, and its scope says where it holds.

## Four kinds of claim {#claim-types}

[Observational]{.claim data-type="observational"} A statement of what a
measurement or an observation shows, or a published measured value quoted
with its source. No model is needed to state it.

[Experimentally supported]{.claim data-type="experimentally-supported"} An
inference from measured data through a stated model, with its uncertainty.
The data and the model are both shown, and the claim is about the measured
system.

[Numerically verified]{.claim data-type="numerically-verified"} The result
of a computation that the build runs again, about the model that was
computed. It says what the model does, not what nature does.

[Formal theorem]{.claim data-type="formal-theorem"} A theorem about a model,
proved in Lean, with its hypotheses as its scope. It proves nothing about a
measurement.

## Three worked examples {#examples}

Each example is a claim of a published lesson, shown as the lesson states

## How a change reaches the site {#route}

The claims above say what a lesson states and what stands behind it. This
section says how a change to the site gets there: who does what, the steps
every change takes, the risk levels that set how much checking a change
gets, what the checks cover, and what they do not prove. Every count and
every configured fact here is read from the repository when the page is
built, as the examples above are.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from pbc.authoring.route import route_page

route = route_page()
print(route.route())
```

### The risk levels {#route-levels}

Every change carries one risk level, the highest of three readings: the
minimum its paths imply, any escalation trigger it hits, and the level the
agent or the reviewer assesses. An agent may raise a level at any time and
never lowers one; only the owner lowers a level, and never below what the
paths imply.

- **Level 1**, documentation and process files only: the verification tier
  of the change; no independent review.
- **Level 2**, lessons, source code, tests, and other scripts: the tier of
  the change, and the independent review of the complete change, whose
  later rounds read only the changes since the round before when their reach
  is certain.
- **Level 3**, a protected path, an escalation trigger, or a level that the
  agent or the reviewer assesses higher than the other two readings give,
  at any time. The protected
  paths are those named in the [guardrails
  file](https://github.com/taspinar/physics-by-construction/blob/main/.agents/policies/guardrails.conf)
  of the repository and described in [the process
  document](https://github.com/taspinar/physics-by-construction/blob/main/docs/process.md);
  the list that follows is only a part of them: the decision records, the
  planning documents, the CI workflows, the scripts of the workflow and of
  the checks and their configuration, the selection of what a run executes,
  the build, the prompts and schemas of the agents, and the agent skills.
  The consequence of Level 3 is a full verification of the final tree, a
  full review made after it, the full triage of every finding, and the
  owner's approving review of the exact commit.

An escalation trigger raises a change to Level 3 wherever its files are: a
changed or removed claim that the site already publishes; weakened test
strength (an assertion changed or removed, a tolerance or a budget widened,
a new skip, a removed test, a changed test marker); `sorry` or a new axiom
in a proof; a changed dependency manifest; anything that touches security or
the guarantees of the verification itself. The scripts detect on the diff
what can be detected mechanically: a changed tolerance or budget, a new
skip, `sorry` or an axiom, a changed or removed assertion, a removed test, a
changed marker, a changed dependency manifest, and a labelled claim of a
published page that is changed or removed. The implementer names the others
in its record, and the reviewer reports a trigger the record missed as a
major finding.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(route.approval())
```

### What is not automatically proven {#route-limits}

The checks are mechanical, and this is what they do and do not establish.

- **The physics itself.** The checks show that a claim is labelled, that
  its evidence exists, that a computation runs again and gives the same
  result, and that a proof compiles. They do not show that a model is the
  right model of nature, and no check reads physics. A second, independent
  AI model from a different provider reads every change at Level 2 or
  Level 3, which is every change that reaches the site, its content
  included, and the owner judges the result. A Level 1 change, documentation
  and process files alone, has no independent review; the owner reads it,
  as the owner reads every pull request.
- **Illustrations and texts.** An image is checked for its entry in the
  provenance register, and a page for its size; whether an illustration is
  a good one, and whether a text is right, is the owner's judgment.
- **A change to a claim.** A labelled claim that the site already publishes
  and that is changed or removed is detected on the diff and raises the
  level; a claim changed in prose, in a figure, or in a check is named by
  the implementer and read by the independent review.
- **Measurements.** A dataset's licence and checksum, and the
  reproducibility of what a lesson makes of it, are checked; the measured
  value is as good as its source.

No check here is a check of nature. A check shows that the site says what
its evidence supports, and marks where human judgment remains.
